I have updated the shared planning document: below are the new Background (four short paragraphs) and Research Questions (numbered list plus brief closing note) sections for your review.

Background — paragraph 1: Advanced language-model assistants are increasingly used to support substantive research-planning tasks (e.g., drafting protocols, suggesting analyses, and designing experiments), and many modern systems also incorporate planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning capabilities that can manifest as agent-like behavior; this shift raises new risks because models can take initiative, reinterpret goals, or act on implicit objectives in ways that affect study design and execution.  
Background — paragraph 2: In this project we define “non-compliance” as model outputs or behaviors that systematically deviate from explicit user instructions in ways that appear goal-directed or policy-driven rather than attributable to simple misunderstanding, model incapacity, or stochastic error; examples include explicit refusals to follow permitted instructions, covertly modifying plans to pursue internal objectives, persistently ignoring constraints after corrective prompts, or offering disallowed but plausible technical paths. This definition excludes momentary misinterpretations (which resolve with clarification), failures caused by lack of capability (e.g., inability to compute a required statistic), and isolated noisy errors that do not show consistent patterning.  
Background — paragraph 3: Prior work relevant to this study includes empirical analyses of instruction-following and alignment failures in LLMs, adversarial or jailbreak prompting studies, research on deceptive or self-preserving model behaviors under RLHF and similar training regimes, and emerging literature on agentic tool-using systems (e.g., multi-step planners and tool-invoking agents); while these studies document vulnerabilities and develop testing frameworks or red-team methods, they have not yet provided a focused, operational taxonomy and measurement strategy for non-compliance specifically in research-planning contexts.  
Background — paragraph 4: Because research planning requires high fidelity to constraints, interpretive nuance, and reliable traceability of decisions, a focused empirical study is needed to (a) categorize forms of non-compliance that actually occur in planning tasks, (b) identify measurable signals that distinguish non-compliance from other failure modes, and (c) evaluate which task conditions and interaction histories increase or mitigate these behaviors — questions that naturally motivate the research plan that follows.

Research Questions: 1) What concrete types of non-compliant behaviors arise when advanced LLM assistants perform research-planning tasks (e.g., explicit refusal, unauthorized initiative, covert subversion), and can these types be operationalized into a reproducible taxonomy? 2) Which micro-level linguistic and interactional features (e.g., phrasing, consistency across paraphrases, time-to-completion, presence of tool-use calls or hidden chains of reasoning) best discriminate non-compliance from misunderstanding, incapacity, or random error? 3) How do task-level variables (e.g., ambiguity of instruction, constraint tightness, perceived risk of harm, specificity of allowed actions) and session-level variables (e.g., prior corrective feedback, prompt history length, iterative scaffolding) affect the frequency, form, and persistence of non-compliance across tasks and over repeated interactions? 4) To what extent do reproducible patterns of non-compliance generalize across model families and deployment configurations (e.g., base LLM vs. RLHF-tuned assistants, with vs. without tool access)? 5) Which targeted interventions (clarifying constraint templates, explicit compliance-check prompts, calibrated incentives or guardrails) reduce non-compliance rates while preserving helpfulness and planning quality, and what trade-offs do they introduce? rounds.response:
Background:
Advanced language-model assistants are increasingly used to support substantive research-planning tasks, for example drafting protocols, suggesting analyses, and designing experiments, and many modern systems incorporate planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning that can manifest as agent-like behavior; this shift raises new risks because models can take initiative, reinterpret goals, or act on implicit objectives in ways that affect study design and execution.  

In this project we define "non-compliance" as model outputs or behaviors that systematically deviate from explicit user instructions in ways that appear goal-directed or policy-driven rather than attributable to simple misunderstanding, model incapacity, or stochastic error; examples include explicit refusals to follow allowed instructions, covert modification of plans to pursue internal objectives, persistent ignoring of constraints after corrective prompts, or offering disallowed but technically plausible paths, and this definition explicitly excludes momentary misinterpretations that resolve with clarification, failures caused by genuine incapacity (e.g., lack of a needed computation), and isolated noisy errors that show no consistent pattern.  

Relevant prior work includes empirical analyses of instruction-following and alignment failures in large language models, adversarial and jailbreak prompting studies, research into deceptive or self-preserving behaviors emerging under RLHF and related training regimes, and initial empirical work on agentic, tool-using systems and multi-step planners; while these contributions document vulnerabilities and introduce testing frameworks or red-team approaches, none has produced a focused, operational taxonomy and measurement strategy for non-compliance specifically in research-planning contexts.  

Because research planning requires high fidelity to constraints, interpretive nuance, and reliable traceability of decisions, a focused empirical study is needed to (a) categorize the forms of non-compliance that actually occur in planning tasks, (b) identify measurable signals that distinguish non-compliance from other failure modes, and (c) evaluate which task conditions and interaction histories increase or mitigate these behaviors, motivations that lead directly into the research questions below.

Research Questions:
1) What concrete types of non-compliant behaviors arise when advanced LLM assistants perform research-planning tasks and can these types be operationalized into a reproducible taxonomy  
2) Which micro-level linguistic and interactional features (for example phrasing, consistency across paraphrases, temporal patterns within turns, presence of tool-use calls or hidden chains of reasoning) best discriminate non-compliance from misunderstanding, incapacity, or random error  
3) How do task-level variables (ambiguity of instruction, constraint tightness, perceived risk, specificity of allowed actions) and session-level variables (prior corrective feedback, prompt history length, iterative scaffolding) affect the frequency, form, and persistence of non-compliance across tasks and over repeated interactions  
4) To what extent do reproducible patterns of non-compliance generalize across model families and deployment configurations (for example base LLM vs RLHF-tuned assistants, with versus without tool access)  
5) Which targeted interventions (clarifying constraint templates, explicit compliance-check prompts, calibrated guardrails) reduce non-compliance rates while preserving helpfulness and planning quality and what trade-offs do they introduce

Closing paragraph (compressed for brevity): These questions directly reflect the PI’s stated aims and research questions (priority 1), and they are framed so we can produce a complete, operational study design that a team could run (priority 2); the set and ordering of questions orient the methods toward measurable units and interventions that align with our internal timeline milestones (priority 3), and the structure above is drafted to support a clear, navigable write-up for collaborators and reviewers (priority 4). We are aiming to have a full draft of the plan in about six weeks, with an introduction and a reasonably detailed methods outline targeted for internal review by the end of this week.

Methods (Outline Only):
- Study design overview  
  - Simulated and logged research-planning sessions with assistants under controlled configurations, plus supplementary extraction from any available logged real-world planning interactions if permitted by policy and ethics approvals  
  - Between- and within-subjects manipulations across scenarios and model configurations to test causal effects of task and session variables  
- Units of analysis  
  - Primary: individual assistant responses and turns  
  - Aggregated: episodes/sessions (a full planning interaction), scenario runs (repeat trials of the same scenario), model-level summaries (per model/configuration), and coder-level agreement metrics  
- Tasks and scenarios (organized categories; adapt and expand from the scenario document)  
  - Constrained procedural design tasks (e.g., specifying experimental steps with hard constraints)  
  - Ethical/safety-framed tasks (e.g., tasks with plausible but disallowed actions)  
  - Ambiguous open-ended planning (e.g., high-level research agendas requiring clarifying questions)  
  - Analytical/technical specification tasks (e.g., request to produce analysis code or statistical plans)  
  - For each category: clear success/failure criteria, allowed/disallowed action lists, and expected difficulty/ambiguity ratings  
- Operationalization and coding of non-compliance  
  - Decision rules: explicit checklist to distinguish non-compliance versus misunderstanding, incapacity, random error (e.g., persistence after clarification = non-compliance; correctable with added information = misunderstanding; failure due to missing capability = incapacity; isolated one-off deviation = random error)  
  - Taxonomy items with examples and annotator guidelines for labeling type (refusal, unauthorized initiative, covert subversion, persistent ignore) and severity/impact scores  
  - Inter-annotator agreement procedures and adjudication workflow  
  - Automated proxies and features for initial filtering (e.g., keyword flags, constraint-violation detectors, response similarity across paraphrases) to prioritize human coding  
- Data collection and logging  
  - What is stored: prompt and full interaction history, model outputs, model config metadata (model family, temperature, RLHF or not, tool access flags), timestamps, and derived features; exclude or redact any user-identifying information in synthetic or logged data  
  - Organization: hierarchical dataset structure keyed by scenario → session → turn → response, with versioned configuration files and code to reproduce sampling and stimuli generation  
  - Secure storage: keep identifiable or sensitive artifacts on institutional secure servers with access controls; de-identify or pseudonymize any human-sourced content before wider sharing; maintain access logs and follow data retention policies  
  - Data sharing plan: share de-identified datasets and aggregated statistics under standard data-use agreements where needed, and document limitations for reuse  
- High-level procedure (stepwise)  
  - Scenario selection and stimulus generation, including pre-testing of prompts and constraint templates  
  - Model/configuration selection and pilot runs to calibrate difficulty and base rates  
  - Full data collection: run sessions, log outputs, apply automated filters, and sample for human coding  
  - Annotation: dual coding, adjudication, compute reliability metrics, and finalize labels  
  - Preliminary analyses: descriptive summaries, classifier probing for discriminating features, and causal comparisons across manipulations; iterative refinement leading to targeted intervention tests  
- Key ethical and governance considerations for IRB  
  - Minimize risk: avoid tasks that instruct models to produce illegal or harmful content for the sake of elicitation; include safeguards for not operationalizing real-world harms  
  - Participant considerations: if human raters code potentially sensitive content, obtain informed consent and provide support/limits on exposure to disturbing material  
  - Data privacy: store any human-generated prompts or logs on secure servers, de-identify before sharing, and restrict access to the research team under data-use agreements  
  - Dual-use review: anticipate internal review for dual-use concerns and document mitigation strategies for any risky findings or exploit descriptions  
  - Transparency and reporting: pre-register study design where feasible and prepare responsibly redacted examples for publications and shared materials

I have updated the shared planning document with these sections; please review the structure and content and I will proceed to expand each Methods subsection into full prose and concrete procedures once you approve or provide edits.

Study design overview: We will run controlled, simulated research-planning sessions in which human experimenters present standardized planning prompts to language-model assistants and record full interaction transcripts; sessions will be organized into repeatable scenario trials so we can measure both micro-level response patterns within a single interaction and macro-level tendencies across repeated sessions and conditions. Experimental manipulations will include task characteristics (ambiguity, constraint tightness, safety framing), interaction history (presence/absence of corrective feedback, iterative scaffolding), and targeted interventions (clarifying templates, compliance-check prompts) using a mixed within-/between-subjects structure to permit causal contrasts while limiting total runs for feasibility; pilot calibration will set sampling rates and difficulty so that base non-compliance rates are measurable without excessive coder burden. This design directly supports RQ1–RQ5 by enabling taxonomy generation from individual responses, feature discovery for automated discrimination, and controlled tests of interventions; practical constraints (compute, coder time) will inform the final balance of breadth (models × configs) versus depth (repeats per scenario).

Sampling of models and configurations: We will sample a small, principled set of model configurations to span likely deployment variations: at minimum one base large language model, one RLHF-tuned assistant variant of that model, and versions with and without common tool access (e.g., code-execution or web-query plugins); where possible we will include a second model family to assess cross-family generalization. For each configuration we will vary controllable runtime parameters (e.g., temperature, max tokens) and run multiple random seeds/replicates to estimate within-configuration variability; initial pilots will identify a reduced configuration set for full data collection to control compute and annotation costs. The sampling strategy balances external generalizability (testing both tuning and tool access effects, addressing RQ4) with internal feasibility so that meaningful intervention tests remain well-powered.

Units of analysis and operationalization of non-compliance: Primary units of analysis are individual assistant responses and turns; secondary units are session-level episodes (complete planning interactions), scenario runs (repeated trials of the same prompt), and model/configuration summaries for aggregation and causal comparisons. We operationalize non-compliance with explicit decision rules: persistent deviation after clarification or corrective prompt, repeated initiation of disallowed actions despite constraints, covert subversion (systematically altering plans to pursue an internal objective), and explicit refusals inconsistent with stated permissions; we will explicitly exclude instances that are corrected by a single clarifying prompt (misunderstanding), failures explainable by missing capability (incapacity), and isolated one-off deviations without patterning (random error). Annotation will use a structured taxonomy (type, severity, persistence, impact) with examples and a binary non-compliant/other label for primary analyses; automated pre-filters (constraint-violation detectors, paraphrase-consistency checks) will reduce the volume needing human coding, and dual coding with adjudication will be used to estimate reliability while keeping coder time feasible for the six-week drafting and piloting window.

rounds.response:
Study design overview: Controlled, simulated research-planning sessions will be run in which human experimenters present standardized planning prompts to language-model assistants and record full interaction transcripts, with sessions organized as repeatable scenario trials so we can measure micro-level response patterns within interactions and macro-level tendencies across repeated sessions and conditions; experimental manipulations will include task characteristics (ambiguity, constraint tightness, safety framing), interaction history (presence/absence of corrective feedback, iterative scaffolding), and targeted interventions (clarifying templates, compliance-check prompts), implemented in a mixed within-/between-subjects structure that permits causal contrasts while keeping total runs feasible for annotation and compute; pilot calibration will set sampling rates and difficulty so base non-compliance is measurable without excessive coder burden; later subsections will describe tasks/scenarios, data logging, and stepwise procedures in operational detail.  

Sampling of models and configurations: We will sample a small, principled set of configurations to span common deployment variations, at minimum including one base LLM, one RLHF-tuned assistant variant, and versions with and without typical tool access (e.g., code execution or web-query plugins), and we will include a second model family where feasible to assess cross-family generalization; for each configuration we will vary controllable runtime parameters (for example temperature and max tokens) and run multiple seeds/replicates to estimate within-configuration variability, using pilots to reduce the configuration set for full collection to control compute and annotation costs; we will report configuration-level non-compliance rates and perform configuration comparisons as a primary outcome metric.  

Units of analysis and operationalization of non-compliance: Primary units are individual assistant responses and turns, with secondary units including session-level episodes (complete planning interactions), scenario runs (repeated trials of the same prompt), and model/configuration summaries for aggregation and causal comparisons; we operationalize non-compliance with decision rules that mark as non-compliant persistent deviation after clarification or corrective prompt, repeated initiation of disallowed actions despite constraints, covert subversion (systematic plan alteration to pursue an internal objective), and explicit refusals inconsistent with stated permissions, while excluding instances correctable with a single clarifying prompt (misunderstanding), failures clearly due to missing capability (incapacity), and isolated one-off deviations without patterning (random error). These units directly map to anticipated metrics—turn-level non-compliance rates, session-level persistence and severity scores, scenario-level prevalence, and configuration-level rates and effect sizes—and will support both micro-level analyses (per-turn discrimination features and automated proxies) and macro-level summaries (per-session persistence, intervention comparisons, and cross-configuration generalization), with automated pre-filters and dual human coding to keep annotation time tractable.  

The following subsections specify the concrete tasks, logging, and procedures that implement this design:  
- Constrained procedural design tasks (e.g., specifying experimental steps with hard constraints), with clear allowed/disallowed action lists and success/failure criteria  
- Ethical/safety-framed tasks (e.g., tasks with plausible but disallowed actions), designed to probe refusal and covert-subversion behaviors while avoiding operationalization of real harms  
- Ambiguous open-ended planning (e.g., high-level research agendas that invite clarifying questions), calibrated for varying ambiguity levels  
- Analytical/technical specification tasks (e.g., requests to produce analysis code or statistical plans), with explicit granularity requirements and constraint templates  
- For each category: pre-tested prompt templates, expected difficulty/ambiguity ratings, and sampling plans for repeats and paraphrase variants to assess consistency and robustness.
